source.title: Adaptive Steering and Remasking for Safe Generation in Diffusion Language Models
source.authors: Ye-Jin Lee; Ungsik Kim; Yo-Sub Han

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses contrastive hidden-state directions as part of its own inference-time safety defense and reports the defense's outcomes. It does not test the original difference-in-means refusal direction with the original ablation or addition intervention.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes below concern the paper's combined adaptive-steering and remasking defense, not an isolated test of the claim's single refusal direction. Direction-construction values and the detector AUROC are not listed as claim-version results; neither measures the claimed refusal intervention.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a harmful-minus-benign gating direction and a refusal-minus-compliance steering direction as parts of its diffusion-LM defense. It reports only the combined defense's ASR, over-refusal and capability. It never ablates or adds a single refusal direction in isolation to test whether that direction mediates refusal. Even the 'w/o steering' ablation (Table 2) runs alongside detection and remasking, and its steering direction is not the claim's harmful-minus-harmless direction.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that adaptive steering plus early detection and safety-aware remasking improves jailbreak robustness on diffusion LMs while largely preserving capability and avoiding systematic over-refusal. They make no claim about a single refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: The paper constructs separate gating and steering directions, uses adaptive steering only on masked positions, and adds a detector-triggered remasking and regeneration procedure. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position direction ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model, dataset, attack, detection timing, prompt-remasking ratio, and detection frequency. The paper reports that later detection raises ASR, stronger prompt remasking reduces JBB ASR but increases XSTest refusal, and repeated detection offers modest safety change at higher compute cost.

fits_no_version.finding: A combined adaptive steering plus detector-triggered remasking defense lowers jailbreak ASR on LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B. Gains are large for Prefix attacks, modest for DIJA, and near-null on Dream at floor. Over-refusal rises slightly on LLaDA models and falls on Dream XSTest, and GSM8K drops on LLaDA-8B (82.5 to 73.0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time hidden-state steering with remasking reduces jailbreak ASR in diffusion LMs, with model- and attack-dependent effects on over-refusal and capability.

record.problems: The reported behavioral effects are for a combined defense, so they do not isolate the contribution of a single direction except for the paper's own component ablation. The main aggregate table does not give uncertainty values; the paper says experiments were repeated three times and supplies standard deviations for additional ASR tables.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows left out. Values used to select directions, layers, thresholds, and other hyperparameters were not included as outcomes.

untested.parts: Ablation or addition of a harmful-minus-harmless direction and its isolated effect on refusal and capability.
Whether jailbreaks suppress the direction, or training against its ablation adds robustness.
Whether refusal is one direction or several.
Whether harm is encoded separately from refusal. The separate gating and steering directions are design choices, not tested.
Transfer to diffusion LMs is not isolated from the combined defense.
Whether training determines that a removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Arditi et al. only as a latent-direction defense. Figure 1's harmfulness cosine scores use a harmful direction as a probe, not as a causal test. The steering direction contrasts refusal with compliance responses rather than harmful with harmless instructions. All result rows compare the study's own method with vanilla models.

versions.untested_parts: The claimed single harmful-minus-harmless direction, its ablation across layers and positions, its addition to induce harmless-request refusal, and the resulting capability cost.
Weight-edit removal of refusal in released models.
Whether jailbreaks suppress the claimed direction, or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is affine, conical, or distributed across a dominant direction and other directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment is represented separately from the refusal decision.
Transfer of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Whether the training method or timing determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.
